title.en: Kusa Jataka: The Ugly Prince and His Fleeing Bride
title.zh: 拘薩本生：醜王子與逃婚的公主

region.en: Kah-gyur narrative India (symbolic pin at Hastinapura)
region.zh: 迦起律典敘事的印度（以哈斯提納普羅為象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. F. Anton Schiefner, done into English by W. R. S. Ralston (1882), ch. II, Kusa Jataka (Kah-gyur vol. ii. pp. 188-192)

summary.en: King Mahasakuni, childless and melancholy, is promised children by Indra, who sends a fertility medicine in a kusa box; the overlooked chief queen drinks the wash-water and bears Kusa, a supremely ugly but mighty Bodhisattva. His bride, tricked into the marriage and horrified at the sight of him, flees home; Kusa follows in disguise, works as chaplet-maker, cook, doctor and soldier, and finally wins her back when he defends her city with the shell, disk and mace Indra gave him, becoming a wheel-turning king with a city of precious stones.
summary.zh: 摩訶薩拘尼王無子而憂，天帝釋因贈靈藥，被忽略的正宮后以拘薩盒洗水飲之，生下極醜而力大的菩薩拘薩。被詭計騙娶的公主一見其貌而逃歸母國；拘薩化名跟隨，歷任花鬘匠、廚師、醫師與武士，最後在城池被困時以帝釋所贈螺、輪、杵退敵，贏回公主，並以四寶建拘薩那竭羅城，成為轉輪王。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature translated in the 19th century; a living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully. Physical ugliness of the hero is part of the traditional tale, not mockery of any community.

passages.text: King Mahasakuni sat leaning his head on his hand, brooding that despite his wealth he would die without son or daughter and his line would be extinguished. The king of the gods, Indra, saw him and promised a medicine: let his wives drink it and they would conceive. The medicine came in a kusa box, and while the chief queen slept the other wives drank and all became pregnant. The queen, furious at being left out, washed the box and drank the water, and she too conceived.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Kusa Jataka (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Her son was born with the eighteen marks of ugliness and a face like a lion's, though of enormous strength; his father's delight in the other sons turned to wrath at him. When rival kings besieged the capital, the boy begged a chariot, and Indra, guarding the Bodhisattva, gave him a shell, a disk and a mace. At one blast of the shell the enemy's ears cracked and their host fled crying that he was a demon; the disk and mace threw whole ranks to the ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Kusa Jataka (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: No family would give a daughter to Kusa, so his father obtained one by a trick, telling another king the marriage was for a different son. Barred from mirrors, from daylight contact with his wife and from stepping-water baths, Kusa was one day seen playing among the youths; his wife asked who the demon was, was told it was her husband, and at night lifted the lamp-cover to see the lion face. She fled to her parents, crying that he was a Pisacha.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Kusa Jataka (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kusa followed her in disguise as a chaplet-maker, a cook and a doctor under different names; each time she saw him she cried Pisacha and he fled. At last, when a hostile prince besieged her father's city, the queen's disguised husband offered to fight. One blast of the shell shattered the besiegers' ears, the princess realized that this champion was Kusa himself, and told her father so. Indra, who had already stopped the despairing hero from hanging himself over his own reflection, showed him four buried treasures; with them Kusa built the jewelled city of Kusinagara and ruled as a mighty Chakravartin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Kusa Jataka (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Adarsamukha, the Prince with the Mirror Face

region.en: Kingdom of King Ananda, Kah-gyur narrative India (symbolic pin at Hastinapura)
region.zh: 阿難王國，迦起律典敘事的印度（以哈斯提納普羅為象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. III, Adarsamukha (Kah-gyur book ii. pp. 198-201)

summary.en: The gentle youngest of five princes, whose face is like a mirror, passes his dying father's threefold succession test - jewel-shoes, immovable throne, steady diadem, recognition by the women, and six divined hidden treasures - and is crowned instead of his hot-tempered brothers. He then judges the chain of misadventures of the Brahman Dandin, punishing the accusers as much as the accused, and solves the questions of the crow, gazelles, partridge, snake and ichneumon, who turn out to be reborn men guarding treasures.
summary.zh: 面如明鏡的幼子阿達薩目卡溫和謙遜，通過臨終父王的三重繼位考驗——寶鞋合足、王座不動、寶冠不移、妃嬪相認，以及以慧力猜出六處秘藏——而越過性情暴躁的兄長們登基。其後他審理婆羅門檀丁一路連環誤傷的訴訟，對原告被告各予懲罰，並解答烏鴉、羚羊、鷓鴣、蛇與獴的提問，揭明牠們皆是執守寶藏的轉生之人。

sensitivity.note: Historical literary corpus (Kah-gyur narrative); nothing restricted reproduced. Note the tale's paradigm of punitive wisdom-judgments belongs to Indian judicial fable absorbed into Tibetan collections.

passages.text: King Ananda had five sons; the youngest was called Adarsamukha, Mirror-face, gentle and modest where his four brothers were rash and hot-tempered. Asked a hard question before the court, the elders could not answer and the youngest answered all. Falling ill, the king devised a test for the succession: the prince whom the jewel-shoes fit, on whom the throne stays firm and the diadem rests steady, whom the women recognize and who can divine the six hidden treasures, should be invested with royal power.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Adarsamukha (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Each elder brother failed: the shoes did not fit, the throne moved, the diadem shook, the women did not know him, and the six treasures - the inner, the outer, the inner-and-outer, the tree-top, the hill-top and the river-shore treasure - eluded him. On Adarsamukha the shoes fitted, the throne stood unmoved, the diadem sat proudly, the women knew him, and he named them all: the treasure inside the threshold, outside it, in the shadow-cast of the king's tree, under the stone in the delight-tank, and at the end of the channel where the water leaves the house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Adarsamukha (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then came the Brahman Dandin, pursued by an impossible chain of accusers: the householder whose borrowed oxen had strayed from the stall, the owner of the mare he stoned to death while trying to stop it, the weaver's wife on whose husband he fell from a wall, the carpenter whose axe dropped into the river when he answered Dandin's question, and the tavern-keeper's baby he unknowingly sat on. Everyone wanted to be taken to King Adarsamukha, who would settle the business.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Adarsamukha (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the road, the crow on the withered tree, the gazelles, a partridge, two fighting snakes-and-ichneumons and a young wife all begged Dandin to carry questions to the king. Adarsamukha judged the oxen case by ordering Dandin's tongue cut out and the householder's eyes put out - and at each judgment the plaintiff preferred to drop the suit rather than suffer his own penalty. To the animals he revealed their former births: the crow had buried a treasure as village headman; the gazelles fed on meadows sweetened by a dripping honey-tree; the snake and ichneumon were two envious brothers hoarding their property, and were told to give their treasures to Sramanas and Brahmans. All obeyed, and Dandin received the wealth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Adarsamukha (1882); not verbatim.

region.en: Hill-town on the Ganges, Kah-gyur narrative India (symbolic pin at Varanasi)
region.zh: 恆河畔山地小鎮，迦起律典敘事的印度（以波羅奈為象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. IV, The Clever Thief (Kah-gyur iv. 132-135)

summary.en: A weaver who thieving by night trains his orphan nephew in the trade; on their first break-in the boy teaches him to go in feet-first - and the uncle is caught by the legs and beheaded by his own apprentice to save himself. The boy then outwits the king at every turn - mourning the corpse disguised as a madman, burning it as a carter, burying its bones in the Ganges as an ascetic - finally fathers a son on the princess and is identified when the infant hands him a wreath; the king, admiring such a hero, marries the thief to his daughter and gives half the kingdom.
summary.zh: 白日織布夜行竊的織工收孤兒為徒；首次破屋時少年教他腳先進——結果叔父被眾人抓住雙腿，徒弟為保己命親手斬其頭。此後少年處處勝過國王：先扮瘋子抱屍痛哭，再扮車夫焚屍滅跡，又扮髑髏外道將骨灰投入恆河；最後與公主有了子嗣，在眾人集會上由嬰兒親手遞上花環而露身。國王嘆服此英雄之才，反將公主嫁他，並分半國為聘。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable with ancient international parallels (Herodotus' Rhampsinitus, ATU-type thief cycles); living Tibetan tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: A widowed mother apprenticed her sharp-witted son to a prosperous weaver. The boy asked why his master ate delicacies and wore fine clothes while he ate coarse food; the weaver answered that he did two kinds of work - weaving by day, thieving by night. To test the nephew he bought a roasted hare, ate one leg in secret, and accused the boy of theft; the youth answered coolly that if the fourth leg was not on the hare it had not gone anywhere. The weaver took him thieving at once.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Clever Thief (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the hole in the house-wall the weaver put in his head first. The youth stopped him: a thief goes in feet-first, for if the head is taken its owner is known and his family ruined. The weaver obeyed, the alarm was raised, and as the crowd pulled him back by the legs the boy, unable to free him, cut off his head and escaped with it. The king exposed the headless trunk at the crossroads, ordering the arrest of anyone who embraced and wailed over it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Clever Thief (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The young thief set out to honor his uncle's body. As a madman he embraced men, women, carts, horses and dogs in the street, until everyone took him for insane - and then he pressed the trunk to his breast, wailed at leisure, and walked away. Next, as a carter, he overturned a cart of dry wood beside the corpse, set fire to it, and burned the body whole. Then as a Brahman he collected alms for soul-offerings and left five oblation-cakes at the burial-place; and last, as an ash-smeared Kapalika, he filled a skull with the bones and ashes and flung it into the Ganges. Each time the king's watchmen identified the trick too late.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Clever Thief (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king staked his daughter in a garden by the river and set watchers on both shores. The thief drew water there for hours in an empty pitcher until the guards took him for a water-carrier; then, covering his head with a pot, he swam down to the garden, stayed with the princess in silence, and left. When her child was born the king assembled all the men of the realm and ordered the infant to crown with flowers the man who was his father - and the boy, walking through the crowd, handed the wreath to the thief. Seized at last, he was nevertheless judged too fine a hero to kill: the king adorned his daughter, gave her to him as wife, and bestowed half the kingdom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Clever Thief (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Naga Janmachitra and the Serpent-Charmer

region.en: Great lake of Hastinapura, North Panchala (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 北般闍羅哈斯提納普羅大湖（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), opening of ch. V, Sudhana Avadana (Kah-gyur ii. 202-209)

summary.en: Fruitful North Panchala owes its harvests to the Naga Janmachitra, whose rain sends the crops up from a great lotus lake. The lawless king of South Panchala, deserted by his own starving people, sets a golden-basket reward for anyone who can conjure the Naga away. A serpent-charmer pegs the lake shore with khadira wood and recites spells until the waters seethe; but the hunter Phalaka, to whom the terrified Naga has fled in man's form, draws a bow on him, forces the spell to be reversed, and kills him - winning the Naga's eternal gratitude and, on the Rishi's advice, the Amogha-chain that holds fast whatever it is cast upon.
summary.zh: 北般闍羅五穀豐登，全賴大蓮花湖中的龍王壽相按時降雨。不守法度的南般闍羅王因百姓逃亡，懸金籃重賞能將龍王攝來之人。捕龍師以吉多羅木釘遍湖岸、誦咒至湖水沸騰；而曾在龍王化人形時庇護他的獵人法勒迦彎弓威脅，逼其解咒，隨即殺之。龍王感恩，獵人又聽仙人之言索得那條「如意索」——擲出即套牢所向之物的寶索。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: In Hastinapura, city of the lawful king Dhana of North Panchala, a great lake full of blue, red and white lotuses was the dwelling of the Naga Janmachitra, who from time to time sent down a torrent of rain; so the land overflowed with rice and sugar-cane and its people gave freely to Sramanas and Brahmans. In lawless South Panchala the god withheld the rain, the towns stood deserted, and the ministers confessed that the people had all fled to the northern king, who ruled with a gentle, benignant and merciful mind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Sudhana Avadana (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The southern king was told the Naga could be conjured away by men versed in charms and spells; he fastened a golden basket to a standard and promised it to whoever should carry Janmachitra off. A serpent-charmer took the offer, went to study the lake, and returned with offerings: within seven days he would capture the Naga.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Sudhana Avadana (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Naga, seeing him, resolved to seek refuge with the hunter Phalaka who lived by the lake. In man's form he came to the hunter, revealed who he was, and gave instructions: when the charmer drove khadira-wood pegs into the four corners of the shore, hung colored threads and recited his spells, the waters would seethe and the Naga be forced forth; then the hunter must bend his bow and order the spell reversed, or the Naga would be bound by it all his life. When the day came the hunter did exactly this, forced the terrified charmer to reverse the spell, and killed him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Sudhana Avadana (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The freed Naga embraced his rescuer - 'you are my mother, you are my father' - and led him to his parents' palace beneath the lake, where he was fed and given jewels. But the Rishi at the nearby hermitage told him what he truly needed: the Amogha-chain, the chain that holds fast, hanging at the entrance of the Naga abode. The Nagas protested it was their defense against the Garuda, but Janmachitra answered his debt and gave it; the hunter carried it home full of joy - and it was this chain that would later snare the Kinnari Manohara.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Sudhana Avadana (1882); not verbatim.

title.zh: 善財童子與緊那羅女美妙

region.en: Hastinapura and the Kinnari kingdom beyond Himavant (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin at Hastinapura)
region.zh: 哈斯提納普羅與雪山地外的緊那羅王國（迦起律典敘事，以哈斯提納普羅為象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. F. A. Schiefner, English by W. R. S. Ralston (1882), ch. V, Sudhana Avadana (Kah-gyur ii. 202-209)

summary.en: The Bodhisattva prince Sudhana is given the kinnari (bird-woman) Manohara, captured by the hunter Phalaka with the Amogha-chain. A treacherous family priest, fearing to lose his post when Sudhana succeeds, tricks the king into a blood-tank rite for which Manohara - a non-human being - is to be killed; warned in time, Sudhana's mother returns the head-jewel and the kinnari flies home to the kingdom beyond Himavant. Sudhana's quest northward through caverns, rams, iron men, whirlpools and demon-haunted rivers, guided by the Rishi and by Manohara's ring dropped in a water-jug, ends in an archery trial before her father Druma and a reunion celebrated in the Kinnari capital.
summary.zh: 菩薩王子善財娶了獵人法勒迦以如意索捕得的緊那羅女美妙。怕失權位的國師設計，慫恿國王舉行血池灌浴之禮，須以「非人」美妙獻祭；王母及時歸還頭珠，緊那羅女凌空歸返雪山之北的故國。善財依仙人所指，歷經洞窟、抵角的公羊、鐵人、六十大匒的漩渦與惡魔盤踞的諸河，以一枚投入水罐的戒指相認，終於在緊那羅王特盧摩面前射穿七棕櫚、七鼓、七豬，贏回妻子。

texts.canonical_translation: F. A. Schiefner, German translation; W. R. S. Ralston, Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, London 1882 (public domain)

narrative.en:
King Dhana of North Panchala, childless, prayed to the gods and a Bodhisattva of the Bhadrakalpa entered his queen's womb; the boy was named Sudhana, given three palaces and three wives, and amused himself in the upper storeys with music. One day the hunter Phalaka, who owed his fortune to the Naga Janmachitra and possessed the Naga's gift, the Amogha-chain that holds fast whatever it is cast upon, met a Rishi at the Brahmasabha pool. The Rishi told him that on the fifteenth of each month Manohara, daughter of Druma king of the Kinnaris, came there with five hundred kinnari companions to bathe, dancing and singing until the very beasts of the forest were enchanted. The hunter hid in the thicket and cast the chain; Manohara bounded and shrieked, her companions fled, and she was secured by her own head-jewel, the jewel by which she flew heavenwards, left in the hunter's hand as a pledge.

Meeting the handsome prince by chance, the hunter offered her to him as a gift. Sudhana looked once and was struck by the dart of passion, 'like a moth falling into the flame'; he carried her home and she became the beloved above all his wives. But a Brahman who had attached himself to Sudhana and feared he would lose his priestly post when the prince took the throne saw his chance when mountaineers rebelled and eight generals had failed: he urged the king to send Sudhana to war and to forbid him a last visit to Manohara. Sudhana left his wife's head-jewel with his mother, with orders to return it only if Manohara's life were in danger. On the campaign the god-king Vaisravana, delayed on his celestial road above the marching prince, sent the yaksha general Panchika to conjure up a phantom host so vast that the mountaineers opened their gates without a battle; Sudhana returned victorious.

That night the king dreamed that a vulture tore open his belly and wound his entrails around the city. The Purohita read the dream as mortal danger and prescribed the cure found in the mystic lore of the Brahmans: a tank a man's height, lined with mortar and filled with the blood of young roes, into which the king must descend while four Veda-learned Brahmans licked his feet and anointed them with the fat of a non-human being. Manohara was that non-human being. When Sudhana's other wives saw the preparations they rejoiced at the promised beauty of the bath, and Manohara, learning from them what it meant, fled to the queen. The queen judged the danger real, gave back the head-jewel with the words that she would now be beyond reproach, and as Manohara was summoned she rose into the air, saying that like a cow freed from its bonds she would flee.

The king feigned satisfaction; Manohara flew first to the Rishi, angrily reminding him that his directions had caused her capture, and left with him a ring and a full account of the way home: three black mountains and three and three beyond, then Himavant himself, then the named range of peaks, a cavern beneath three of them, the king of birds carrying the traveler over Vajraka, ram-like magic creatures, the Rakshasa Pingala, a black snake in the cavern to be shot with the bow, two rams whose horns must be broken to find the way, iron men with fear-inspiring weapons, an iron-lipped Rakshasi to be pinned with a wedge at the forehead, a whirlpool fount of sixty fathoms, the lion-yellow-haired Yakshas and Rakshasas, and the rivers Crocodile, Butterfly, Sad, Gay, Weeper, Laugher, snake-filled and reed-filled - each with its own charm or courage or silence to cross. Then the capital of the Kinnari king.

Sudhana returned from the war and learned what had happened. His father offered him a more beautiful wife; he refused, and when the gates were guarded he left by night, addressing his laments to the moon, a gazelle, the bees, a snake, a kokila bird and the asoka tree. At the hermitage the Rishi welcomed him, gave him the ring, and repeated the way, together with the provisions needed: the nectar remedy boiled in butter that banishes hunger and thirst, a monkey to carry, spells to learn, bow and arrows, a gleaming jewel, poison and antidote, three iron wedges and a lyre. Provided with all these, Sudhana crossed the rivers and the caverns and came near Druma's city.

Kinnari water-carriers told him the jugs they bore were to wash the smell of humanity off the captive-princess-turned-returned-daughter; asking whether the jugs would be emptied all at once or one by one, he dropped his ring into one jug and asked that it be poured first. The ring fell into Manohara's lap. The king, whose first answer to 'what would you do with the youth Sudhana' had been to cut him into a hundred pieces, cooled; Manohara dressed her husband in divine array and set seven golden stems, seven palms, seven kettledrums and seven boars as the trial. Sudhana sliced the golden stems like a plantain and shot a single arrow uninjured through the seven palm-trees, the seven kettledrums and the seven boars, standing unmoved afterwards like Sumeru. Set among a thousand identical kinnaris, Manohara stepped forward at his truthful verse. Druma gave her back with a jar of gold-dust, warning only that men are fickle. When homesickness later drew the pair back to Hastinapura, they flew through the air by kinnari power; Sudhana told his father everything, was invested with royal power, and for twelve years offered sacrifice without hindrance.
narrative.notes: Cultural function: the tale is the Tibetan Kah-gyur's version of the Kinnari-Manohara cycle; it teaches the inviolability of the marriage vow against paternal realpolitik, models the hero's quest through enumerated trials (a form saturated into Himalayan storytelling), and folds the Naga-gratitude subplot into a single chain of debt and gift.

functions: Models the Bodhisattva's constancy: the prince holds to his wife against king, priest and state religion alike
Paradigm of the enumerated quest - the way home is given as a list of named trials, a structure recycled across Himalayan and Southeast Asian tellings
Explains ritual distrust of Brahmans/Purohitas: the family priest's blood-tank rite is exposed as self-serving fraud
Links three realms (human, Naga lake, Kinnari mountain kingdom) into one economy of debt, gift and rescue

variants.name: Pali and Southeast Asian recensions of the Manohara cycle
variants.text_tradition: Pali Jataka tradition and Thai/Lao-Khmer Manora-Phra Suthon tellings
variants.summary: The capture-by-feather-or-jewel, flight, and quest-after-the-fleeing-wife are told of the same kinnari across Pali, Thai (Phra Suthon-Manora) and Khmer recensions; the Tibetan Kah-gyur version is the earliest printed full narrative, with the Naga Amogha-chain subplot elaborated.

variants.name: Tibetan Manohara stupa-tale (Bhutan/Dochula tradition)
variants.summary: In Bhutan the story is localized: the fleeing Manohara is remembered at Dochula/Dochu-la near Thimphu, where the Kinnari is said to have left her son and the stupa legend fixes the plot on the landscape.

variants.name: Schiefner's German and Ralston's English
variants.summary: Ralston's English (1882) renders Schiefner's German; the celebrated 60-fathom whirlpool and river-names passage was flagged by both translators as obscure, and modern readers treat the river list as symbolic rather than geographic.

texts.sensitivity_guidance: The Manohara story remains part of living Buddhist narrative in Tibet, Bhutan and the Himalayas; all passages below are paraphrases of the 1882 public-domain translation, not verbatim reproduction, and the tradition is treated respectfully.

sensitivity.note: Living Buddhist narrative tradition (Kah-gyur); paraphrase of public-domain 1882 translation only; nothing restricted reproduced.

passages.text: On the fifteenth of the month, Manohara, daughter of Druma the Kinnari king, came with five hundred kinnari companions to the Brahmasabha pool to bathe, dancing and singing so sweetly that even the beasts of the forest were enchanted - the Rishi who told the hunter of it said the sound gave him delight for seven whole days. The hunter hid in the thicket with the Amogha-chain he had won from the Naga, and cast it: Manohara bounded and shrieked, her companions fled, and the hunter secured her by her own head-jewel, the jewel by which she flew heavenwards, which she had left with him as a pledge of good faith.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Sudhana Avadana (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The hunter offered her to Prince Sudhana, who looked once and was struck by the dart of passion, like a moth falling into the flame. When mountaineers rebelled and eight generals had failed, the Purohita urged the king to send his son to war and forbid him a last sight of Manohara. Sudhana left her head-jewel with his mother: give it back only if her life is in danger. The campaign was won without a fight, for the god Vaisravana, delayed on his celestial road above the marching prince, sent the yaksha general Panchika to raise a phantom host so vast the mountaineers opened their gates at once.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Sudhana Avadana (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king dreamed that a vulture tore open his belly and wound his entrails around the city. The Purohita read it as mortal danger and prescribed the Brahmans' mystic cure: a tank filled with the blood of young roes, into which the king must descend while four Veda-learned Brahmans licked his feet and anointed them with the fat of a non-human being - and Manohara was that non-human being. Learning what the bath meant, she fled to the queen, who gave back the head-jewel; and as she was summoned she rose into the air, saying that like a cow freed from its bonds she would flee.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Sudhana Avadana (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: She flew first to the Rishi, telling him his directions had caused her capture, and left with him a ring and the way home: three black mountains, and three and three beyond, then Himavant, a cavern beneath three peaks, the king of birds carrying the traveler over Vajraka, ram-like creatures, the iron men, the iron-lipped Rakshasi to be pinned with a wedge, the whirlpool of sixty fathoms, the demon rivers, then the Kinnari king's capital. Sudhana, armed with the nectar remedy, a monkey, spells, bow, jewel, poison and antidote, three wedges and a lyre, crossed them all and dropped his ring into a water-carrier's jug - the first to be poured over the restored princess. It fell into Manohara's lap.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Sudhana Avadana (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Before her father Druma, Sudhana sliced seven golden stems like a plantain and shot one arrow uninjured through seven palm-trees, seven kettledrums and seven boars, standing unmoved afterward like Sumeru. Set among a thousand identical kinnaris, Manohara stepped forward at his truthful verse; Druma gave her back with a jar of gold-dust, warning only that men are fickle. Later, homesick, the pair flew back through the air to Hastinapura; Sudhana told all, was invested with royal power, and for twelve years offered sacrifice without hindrance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Sudhana Avadana (1882); not verbatim.
